narrative:
Your promotion was denied because the model estimated a 57% chance you will leave your job—slightly more likely than not. This probability reflects patterns in job-related factors, not a certainty or a judgment of your value.

The strongest factor influencing the prediction was your participation in training programs, and it actually pushed toward staying: you attended seven or more programs in the last three years, while most employees attended fewer (about a third had none, and another third had one to three). That high engagement worked in your favor. However, two experience factors outweighed it and pushed toward leaving. Your overall work experience of 6–10 years is longer than the most common group (half of employees predicted to stay have only 1–5 years), and your tenure in your current organization of 1–5 years is also typical of the majority but still signals a relatively short stay that the model associated with higher departure risk. Together, these experience factors tipped the balance just above 50%.

What should happen next? The organization should treat this as a retention signal, not a final verdict. A conversation about your career path, promotion criteria, and what would keep you engaged is warranted—especially given your strong training participation. You may also want to clarify expectations for advancement and discuss how your growing experience can be recognized, so the model’s concern about departure is addressed directly.
